sections.title: The sixth and final paragraph of the Introduction states the point of attachment for the whole inquiry. Husserl proposes — not inappropriately, he says — to attach the treatment of the problems just roughly indicated (to which several others will intimately attach themselves) to the descriptive-psychological distinction of several concepts of consciousness (Bewußtsein) that flow into one another. He notes the customary phrasings: psychic acts are often called "activities of consciousness," "relations of consciousness to a content (object)," and sometimes "consciousness" is defined outright as a collective expression for psychic acts of every kind. The ambiguity of "consciousness" will therefore be the doorway through which the analysis of intentional experience is entered — which is exactly the program of the First Chapter.

sections.title: The tenth paragraph is the second-edition Addendum explicitly relativizing the whole quarrel. It is to be expressly emphasized, Husserl says, that the position taken here on the question of the pure ego (the position he no longer endorses) remains irrelevant for the investigations of this volume. However important this question is otherwise, and as a purely phenomenological question, the most comprehensive problem-spheres of phenomenology — those concerning, in a certain generality, the real content of intentional experiences and their essential relation to intentional objects — can be subjected to systematic investigation without taking any position at all on the ego-question. The present investigations restrict themselves exclusively to such spheres. With regard to the fact that so significant a work as the recently appeared first volume of the second redaction of Natorp's Introduction to Psychology engages with the above expositions, Husserl has not simply struck them. The chapter thus closes with a methodological firewall: the result of the entire Fifth Investigation does not stand or fall with the ego-doctrine debated in this opening chapter.

sections.title: The eleventh paragraph confirms by the earlier identity-series and leaves room for descriptive differences. To confirm the conception of the meaning-essence (meaning in concreto), Husserl recalls the identity-series by which (in the First Investigation) the unity of meaning was separated from the unity of objectivity, and the frequent examples of expressive experiences serving to illustrate the general conception of the intentional essence. The identity of "the" judgment or "the" assertion lies in the identical meaning that repeats itself in the manifold single acts precisely as the same and is represented in them by the meaning-essence. That a wide latitude remains open here for very considerable descriptive differences regarding other components of the acts, Husserl has set out at length.

What has just been set out does not, of course, exclude that (as already touched) a distinction is drawn between the object simpliciter, which is in each case intended, and the object as it is thereby intended (in what apprehension-sense and possibly in what "fullness" of intuition), and that to the latter title its own analyses and descriptions belong. The thesis of identity holds for the object which is intended; it leaves room for the rich descriptions of the object as intended.

sections.title: The fifth paragraph rejects this: matter is abstract and cannot occur in isolation. On attentive essence-consideration of the relevant experiences, it seems unavoidable to grasp the mere presenting really as an act. The interweaving of matters with act-qualities is, as we convince ourselves on the basis of exemplary intuition, an interweaving of abstract moments. Hence isolated, the matter cannot occur; it can evidently gain concretion only in supplementation by arbitrary moments lawfully delimited by the highest genus act-quality. To be sure, the mere understanding — in general the mere "having-put-forward" — is something quite essentially other than the "positing" of belief or other "position-takings" of surmising, wishing. But then we have precisely to recognize, and phenomenologically fix, differences within the total genus act-quality. (A footnote refers to Ideen I, §109, on the "qualitative modification"/"neutrality-modification," noting that deeper insight there required developments of the doctrine of "act-quality" which leave the essential content of this chapter untouched but bring a partial reinterpretation of the results won.) Mere presenting is thus not a non-act bearing isolated matter, but itself an act-quality, a distinctive species within the genus — the positionless counterpart of belief and the other position-takings.

sections.title: The third paragraph identifies the different sources of the universal nominal foundation. For so we can also view the matter: the circumstance that no matter is possible without objectivating quality must itself have the consequence that, where a matter is founded in other matters, an objectivating act of the first matter is also founded in just such acts of the latter matters. Thus the fact that every act is at all times founded in nominal acts has different sources. The original source lies everywhere in this: that every simple matter (including no further material founding) is a nominal one, and accordingly every last-founding objectivating act is a nominal one. But since all other-kinded act-qualities are founded in objectivating ones, the last founding by nominal acts transfers from the objectivating to all acts whatever.
